memories.text: Notes from the heat pump handover with Brightwater Heating on 10 February 2026. The outdoor unit sits in the side passage on a concrete plinth with rubber anti-vibration feet; keep a clear metre in front of the fan and never cover it, even in snow, and brush leaves off the grille in autumn. The controller lives in the hall cupboard beside the hot water cylinder, with the paper manual in a plastic sleeve on the door. The installer set a weather curve of 0.5, with a flow temperature of 45 degrees when it is minus 3 outside, which suits the two larger radiators fitted in the back bedroom and the lounge. The system pressure gauge under the cylinder should read between 1 and 1.5 bar when the heating is cold; if it falls below 0.8 bar, top it up with the silver filling loop until the needle reaches 1.2, then close both taps again and write the date in the logbook. The magnetic filter on the return pipe needs cleaning once a year, ideally in September before the heating season starts: switch off at the isolator, close the two valves either side, unscrew the cap and rinse the magnet under the tap, then open the valves slowly. Leave the radiator valves fully open in every room; the heat pump works best with low, steady heat and no room turned off completely. The hot water cylinder heats overnight in the cheap hours and runs its legionella cycle on Sunday mornings. Defrost cycles are normal in damp, cold weather: the fan stops, the unit steams for a few minutes and then starts again by itself. Error code H7 on the controller means the outdoor unit has lost power; check circuit 5 at the consumer unit before calling anyone. The warranty runs for seven years as long as the annual service is done, and the first service is due in February 2027. The grant paperwork and the commissioning certificate are filed in the blue folder on the bookshelf in the lounge. If the controller shows a padlock symbol, the installer's holiday lock is on; hold the menu button for ten seconds to clear it. For any question in the first year, ring the installer's aftercare line before booking anyone else, or the warranty may not cover the visit.

memories.author: sam
memories.text: Notes from the catalogue migration meeting at the library on 13 October 2026. The old catalogue system goes read-only at 5 pm on Friday 20 November and the new one opens to the public on Monday 30 November, so for one week loans are written on paper slips and typed in afterwards. Sam leads the data side: export the 48,000 item records, the 6,200 borrower records and the open loans, check the counts against the old system, and fix the records with broken barcodes before the import. The vendor runs two trial imports, on 3 and 10 November, into a test copy; each one is checked against a list of 200 sample items picked at random from the shelves. If the final import fails, or the counts differ by more than 0.5 per cent, the fallback is to keep the old catalogue running read-write for another week and try the import again on Friday 27 November. Borrowers keep their card numbers, so nobody needs a new card. Reservations made before the switch are carried over, but the queue order is checked by hand for the 40 most reserved titles. The self-service machines are switched off during the paper week and come back with the new software. The children's library keeps its own sticker system for reading challenges, which is not part of the migration at all. Training for the front desk is on 23 and 24 November, two sessions each day, and the volunteers get a short talk from Sam on 19 November. Posters announcing the change go up on 2 November, with a note on the website and in the newsletter. Questions from borrowers go to a shared inbox that Sam checks twice a day during the switch. The budget covers the vendor's import days and two extra hours a week for the volunteers until Christmas. After the switch the old server is kept, switched off, for three months and then wiped. Sam's own checklist for the paper week: print 500 loan slips, keep a copy of the borrower list on the locked laptop at the desk, and count the slips every evening against the returns trolley. The mobile library van keeps running during the switch with its own paper slips, and its loans are typed in last.

memories.author: sam
memories.text:
Wickmere beekeepers: hive inspection guide for the two hives at the Fallow Lane orchard.

When. From April to September each hive is inspected every seven to nine days, on a warm, still afternoon above 15 °C, so the foragers are out. From October to March nobody opens a hive: heft it from behind once a fortnight to feel how much store is left, and look at the entrance on a sunny day.

Kit. Veil and gloves, the hive tool and the smoker. Light the smoker with dry wood shavings and keep it going with a handful of dry grass. The spare smoker and a tin of fuel are kept in the green bin under the bench in the orchard shed, beside the spare frames.

Order. Stand to one side of the entrance, puff a little smoke in, wait a minute, then lift the roof and crown board. Take out the first frame from the edge and work across the box one frame at a time, holding each over the hive so a dropped queen falls back in. Put every frame back in the order it came out.

What to look for. Eggs standing up in the cells mean a laying queen was there within three days. Look for the queen herself only if there are no eggs. Count frames of brood and of stores, and write both on the record card pinned inside the roof. Queen cells along the bottom of a frame in May or June mean the colony is getting ready to swarm: tell the group the same day.

No queen. If a colony has no eggs and no young brood for two inspections in a row, it has lost its queen. Do not wait for it to fix itself: take a frame of eggs from the stronger hive and put it in the middle of the queenless brood box, so the bees can raise a new queen, and check again after a week. Tell the group on the chat.

Temper. A colony that follows you down the path or stings through the gloves is noted on the card, and the next visit goes in pairs.

Feeding. A hive that feels light when hefted in October gets a block of fondant on the crown board; no syrup is given after mid September. Write the date on the card.

After. Close the hive, write the card, and clean the hive tool in washing soda before the next hive, so nothing passes between colonies.

notes.title: Sabbatical walk plan
notes.text:
# Sabbatical walk plan

The plan for spring 2027: walk the whole coast path from Wrenmouth to the far end at Cape Tallow in about ten weeks, with a rest day every sixth day and no more than 25 km on any single day.

## Money

Save 400 GBP a month until March 2027. Budget 55 GBP a day for food and beds, less on camping nights, and keep 300 GBP aside for a train home if anything goes wrong.

## Kit

- 38 litre pack, under 9 kg loaded without water.
- Two litres of water as standard, and three litres on the long stages with no café or tap, such as Saltreach to Gullhaven and the whole moorland edge.
- Lightweight tent for the wild stretches, with a bivvy bag as a backup.
- Waterproof jacket and over-trousers, and two pairs of walking socks for every day of rain.
- First aid kit with blister plasters, tape and the knee support.
- Head torch, power bank and the paper maps in a waterproof case.

## Route

- Week 1: Wrenmouth to Marram Point, stages 1 to 3 in the coast path stages note.
- Week 2: Marram Point to Brindle Head, with the first rest day at the youth hostel in Pellow Cove.
- Week 3: the cliff section; book the ferry across the Torrin estuary a day ahead, because it only runs around high tide.
- Weeks 4 to 6: the long beaches, flat but slow on soft sand; start early to avoid the midday heat.
- Weeks 7 to 9: the moorland edge, the hardest climbs of the walk; resupply in Hatherby Market.
- Week 10: the last 60 km to Cape Tallow, with a rest day before the final stage.

## Practical

- Post a resupply box to the youth hostel in Pellow Cove and another to the post office in Hatherby Market.
- Keep a paper map for the moorland, where the phone signal is poor.
- Send Sam the route for the week every Sunday evening.
- Ask the hostels about drying rooms when booking.

## Before leaving

- Tell Larkspur Labs at least four months ahead, as the engineering handbook asks.
- Get the boots resoled and buy new insoles in January.
- Do two weekend test walks with the full pack in February, one of them on the moorland.
- Leave the tent and stove instructions with Sam in case a parcel has to be sent on.

# Winter concert

Saturday 12 December 2026 in the main hall of the Corn Exchange. Doors open at 6.30 pm, the concert starts at 7 pm and should finish by 9.15 pm.

## Programme

- First half: four winter carols, the Breton lullaby with the children's choir, and the sea shanty medley.
- Interval: 20 minutes, with mulled apple juice and mince pies from the bake sale team.
- Second half: the commissioned piece Lanterns on the Quay, then the audience carols.

## Rehearsals

- Thursdays at 7 pm upstairs at the Corn Exchange, as usual.
- An extra sectional for the altos on Sunday 29 November, 2 to 4 pm.
- Dress rehearsal on Friday 11 December at 6 pm in the main hall; arrive by 5.45 to warm up.

## What to wear

Black trousers or a black skirt, black shoes, and the dark green scarves handed out in October. No perfume, for the sake of the singers with asthma.

## Jobs

- The tenors bring the music stands from the store on the Friday afternoon.
- The sopranos set out the chairs: 180 of them, in rows of 12 with a centre aisle.
- Sam runs the ticket table with the cash box and the card reader.
- The basses take the stands back to the store on Monday morning.

## Tickets

12 GBP, or 6 GBP for under-16s, on sale from 1 November at the library desk and on the door.

## Notes to self

- Learn the alto line of the second verse of the lullaby by heart.
- Ask at work whether the poster can go in the library window.
- Bring throat sweets and a bottle of water.
- Charge the card reader on Friday night.

## Bake sale

The choir's own bake sale is on Saturday 21 November in the Corn Exchange foyer, to pay for the hall hire. Sam's two trays of tarts go on the left table with the price cards. Takings go in the second cash box, separate from the ticket money, and the treasurer banks both on the Monday.

## After the concert

- Stack the chairs at the side of the hall in tens.
- Sweep the stage and check the green room for lost scarves.
- The committee counts the money in the office and writes the total in the choir's book.
- The hall must be empty by 10.30 pm, or the Corn Exchange charges for another hour.

notes.author: sam
notes.title: Garden plan 2027
notes.text:
# Garden plan 2027

What we agreed for the back garden next year. The allotment stays Sam's own project; this is the garden at home.

## Beds

- Two new raised beds along the south fence, 2.4 m by 1.2 m each, built from the leftover oak sleepers in March.
- Fill them with the compost from the bins by the shed and 40 bags of topsoil.
- The old herb bed by the back door stays, but the mint goes into a pot before it takes over again.

## Trees and fruit

- Plant a dwarf apple and a dwarf pear on the lawn side in February, both on dwarfing rootstock.
- Move the gooseberry bush from the shady corner to the end of the new beds.
- Net the redcurrants by June, or the blackbirds take them all.

## Lawn

- Leave a strip by the hedge unmown until August for the wildflowers.
- Reseed the bare patch where the paddling pool stood all summer.

## Water

- A second water butt on the garden office gutter.
- A drip line for the raised beds on a timer from the outside tap, which still has to be drained every November.

## Wildlife

- A hedgehog gap at the bottom of the fence on the side of number 9.
- Two bird boxes on the garden office wall, facing north-east.
- No slug pellets anywhere in the garden.

## Budget

About 450 GBP in total: the sleepers are already paid for, topsoil 160 GBP, the two trees 90 GBP, the drip line and timer 70 GBP, the water butt 45 GBP, and the rest for seeds and young plants.

## Order of work

1. February: plant the trees.
2. March: build the raised beds and fill them.
3. April: drip line and the first seeds in the beds.
4. May: the second water butt and the bird boxes.

## Compost

- Turn the two compost bins in March and October.
- Kitchen scraps only in the left bin, garden waste in the right one.
- The finished compost goes on the raised beds before planting.

## Not doing this year

- No pond: the hedgehog gap and the bird boxes come first.
- No new shed; the old one gets a coat of preservative in May instead.
- The patio stays as it is until the kitchen is paid off.

## Questions

- Ask the neighbours at number 9 whether the fence panel on their side can be replaced at the same time.
- Check whether the drip line timer needs a battery or can run from the garden office.

documents.title: House manual
documents.text:
House manual. This is the household's own guide to the house: what lives where, who to call and what to do when something goes wrong. Keep it up to date when anything changes.

Heating. The heat pump runs on a weather curve; leave the thermostat at 20 degrees and let it work slowly. The outdoor unit needs a clear metre in front of it, so keep the bikes on the other side of the passage. In very cold weather it runs a defrost cycle and steams for a few minutes; that is normal. The hot water cylinder heats to 50 degrees every night and to 60 degrees on Sundays for the legionella cycle.

Windows and doors. The back door sticks in wet weather; lift the handle as you turn the key. The skylight on the landing opens with the long pole kept behind the airing cupboard door. The front door has a second lock that is never used; the key for it is lost and nobody should worry about it.

Garden. The water butt by the shed fills from the shed roof only. The outside tap is on the back wall and must be drained before the first frost: close the inside valve under the kitchen sink, then open the outside tap until it stops dripping. The compost bins are emptied in April and October. The hedge is cut after the birds have finished nesting, never before August.

Kitchen. The extractor fan filter is washed every month in hot soapy water. The dishwasher salt goes in the round cap at the bottom left. If the dishwasher shows error E15 it has a leak in its base: switch it off at the wall and tilt it gently back to drain the tray. The fridge freezer is set to 4 and minus 18 degrees.

Electricity. The consumer unit is in the cupboard by the front door. Circuit 1 is the cooker, circuit 2 the ring main downstairs, circuit 3 the ring main upstairs, circuit 4 the lights, circuit 5 the heat pump and circuit 6 is the garden office at the end of the garden. If a circuit trips, unplug everything on it before switching it back on. The meter readings are taken on the first of each month and written in the weekly review note.

Water. The water stopcock is under the stairs, behind the vacuum cleaner, and turns clockwise to close. There is a second stopcock in the street under the small square cover by the gate; it needs the long key that hangs inside the meter cupboard. The water meter is read on the first of each month with the electricity.

Who to call. For the heat pump call the installer first; for the boiler there is nothing to call any more. For the roof and gutters the household uses a local firm whose card is pinned inside the meter cupboard. The neighbours at number 9 hold a spare key to the shed, not to the house.

documents.title: Hollin Vey owner's guide notes
documents.text:
Hollin Vey owner's guide notes, kept by the household from the dealer handover. Order HV-208815, collected on 14 June 2026, blue, with the 64 kWh battery.

Range. The dealer quoted about 250 miles in summer and about 190 miles in a cold winter with the heater on. Preconditioning the cabin while the car is still plugged in saves range on frosty mornings, and so does keeping the tyres at the right pressure.

Charging at home. The wall box on the side wall is set to charge from midnight to 5 am, when the tariff is cheapest. A full charge from 20 per cent takes about six and a half hours. The charging cable locks into the car while it charges: to release it, unlock the car twice with the key fob, or press the small release button in the boot above the left tail light.

Public charging. The car takes CCS rapid chargers up to 100 kW; 10 to 80 per cent takes about 35 minutes. The charging card is in the glovebox with the paper logbook.

Tyres. The car came with all-season tyres at 36 psi front and rear. Check them on the first Sunday of each month at the air pump by the supermarket.

Twelve-volt battery. If the car will not wake up, the small battery under the front panel may be flat; the jump terminals are behind the cover marked with a plus sign.

Service. Every two years or 20,000 miles at the dealer in Saltreach, and brake fluid every three years. Software updates arrive overnight over the home Wi-Fi when the car is parked on the drive.

Breakdown. The car includes three years of roadside assistance from the maker; the number to call is on the sticker inside the charging flap.

Keys. The spare key lives in the kitchen drawer with the takeaway menus, never in the car. If a key fob battery runs low, the car shows a warning and the key still works when held against the steering column.

Winter. Clear snow from the charging flap before plugging in, and park nose-out on the drive so the cable reaches the wall box without stretching. Below minus 10 degrees the range drops faster than the dealer's winter figure, and the seat heaters use far less energy than the cabin heater.

documents.title: Nettlebank Allotment Society handbook
documents.text:
Nettlebank Allotment Society handbook. Welcome to Nettlebank. This handbook explains how the site works; the shorter rules sheet for the year is sent out separately each January.

Plots and rent. Full plots are 250 square metres and half plots 125. Rent is due by 30 November each year: 45 GBP for a half plot and 80 GBP for a full plot, paid to the treasurer or into the society's account.

Water. Each row of plots shares a trough filled from the mains between April and October. Water butts are encouraged; plot holders may fit up to four, connected to a shed or greenhouse roof. Hosepipes are not allowed in the summer months.

Sheds and structures. A plot may have one shed up to 2.4 by 1.8 metres and one greenhouse or polytunnel. Ask the committee before building anything else.

Animals. Plot holders may keep up to six hens on a full plot, never a cockerel, and bees only after the society's beekeeping course.

Bonfires. Bonfires are allowed only in November, after 4 pm, and must be put out before you leave the site.

Untended plots. A plot that is not worked for three months receives a warning letter. After a further two months without improvement the tenancy ends and the plot is offered to the next person on the waiting list.

Paths and edges. Keep the paths beside your plot mown and clear; the shared main path is mown by volunteers on the first Saturday of the month.

Tools. The tool store by the gate holds a petrol mower, two strimmers and a rotavator, booked in the logbook; return them clean and with fuel.

Manure. Free horse manure is delivered in October and heaped at the bottom of the site; take what you need with a wheelbarrow.

Security. Lock the gate behind you every time. The gate code changes each spring and is sent to plot holders by post.

Events. The produce show is held in the second week of August and the bring-and-share supper in September.

Committee. The committee meets on the first Wednesday of each month in the hut, and the minutes are pinned to the noticeboard.

documents.title: Larkspur Labs engineering handbook
documents.text:
Larkspur Labs engineering handbook, audio team section.

How we ship. The desktop editor ships every six weeks on a release train. A release candidate is cut on the Monday and tagged on the Thursday after the listening tests pass. Tickets use the RHY prefix and every fix names its ticket in the commit message. Hotfixes outside the train need the approval of that cycle's release captain and a second reviewer from the audio team; they ship as a patch build within 48 hours.

Encoders and dependencies. Encoder and resampler versions are pinned in the build manifest and only changed in their own pull request with a benchmark attached: render the twelve reference projects and compare loudness, peaks and render time against the previous build.

On call. Each engineer is on call for one week at a time, Monday to Monday, about once every eight weeks. The on-call engineer watches the crash reports and the support queue but is never expected to work at night.

Working hours. Core hours are 10 am to 4 pm. The Saltreach office is open every weekday and people choose their office days with their lead.

Equipment. Laptops are replaced every three years. Studio headphones and an audio interface are issued on the first day and stay with the team when you leave.

Learning. Everyone has five learning days a year and a budget of 600 GBP for courses or conferences; ask your lead before booking.

Leave. Annual leave is 27 days plus public holidays, and up to five days carry over to the next year.

Sabbaticals. After two full years of service you may take an unpaid sabbatical of up to three months. Ask at least four months ahead; your role is kept open while you are away.

Communication. Decisions are written up in the team's decision log, and a meeting without notes did not happen. Questions go in the team channel rather than in private messages, so the answers help the next person.

Security. Never paste customer audio into outside tools, keep test projects synthetic, and report a lost laptop on the same day.

documents.title: Fieldhouse Audio Summit programme
documents.text:
Fieldhouse Audio Summit, Leeds, 16 to 18 November 2026. Speaker programme, as sent to speakers.

Monday 16 November. Registration opens at 1 pm at the Corn Mill venue, and the welcome session is at 3 pm. The speakers' dinner is at 7.30 pm on Monday in the mill's upstairs gallery; dress is smart casual.

Tuesday 17 November. The morning keynote at 9.30 is on loudness standards. Track A covers mixing tools and track B covers codecs and transport. Alex speaks in track B at 11.40 on Tuesday, in Room 3: Pinning encoders without fear, 25 minutes plus 5 minutes of questions. Slides must be uploaded as a PDF by 6 pm on Sunday 15 November. The room has an HDMI adapter but no audio interface, so bring your own if the demo needs one. Lunch is served from 12.30 to 1.30 on both full days. Tuesday afternoon has hands-on workshops that need booking at the desk. The conference dinner for all attendees is on Tuesday at 7 pm at the boat club by the canal, a short walk from the venue.

Wednesday 18 November. Lightning talks start at 9.30, the panel on open audio formats is at 11, and the closing remarks are at 1 pm. The venue closes at 3 pm.

Travel. The venue is a ten-minute walk from the station. Speakers' expenses cover two nights at the partner hotel, booked by the organisers in the speaker's name, and standard-class train travel booked by the speaker and claimed afterwards with receipts.

Accessibility. There is step-free access to every room, a quiet room on the ground floor and live captioning in the main hall.

Other. The Wi-Fi details are printed on the back of the badge. Recordings of track B talks are published two weeks after the event if the speaker agrees on the release form.

For speakers. Arrive at Room 3 fifteen minutes before your slot to test the projector with the technician. The session chair holds up cards at five minutes and at one minute left. Questions are taken from the room microphone only, so repeat each question before answering it, for the recording. Speakers get a free ticket for one guest on the Wednesday.
